lede: Waves are how energy gets from one place to another without anything being carried there. Ripples on a puddle, a shout across a field, light from a star: all the same idea, described by four measurements and one equation.
can: Tell a transverse wave from a longitudinal one by how the particles vibrate
Read the amplitude and wavelength off a distance graph and the frequency off a time graph
Use v = f λ any way round, with the units converted before you substitute

md: Drop a stone into a puddle and rings spread outwards, but the water stays where it was. Shout across a field and your voice reaches somebody who never moved. Both are waves: something travels, and it is not the stuff in the way.

caption: Follow the dot. It moves up and down and stays put; the shape is what travels.

md: A wave carries **energy** from one place to another, and it does it by making the material in the way **vibrate**. Watch one point on the rope in the picture: it moves up and down about the same spot while only the energy travels along. Here the vibration is **at right angles to** the direction the wave travels, so this is a **transverse** wave. Water waves and every electromagnetic wave are transverse.

stem: A cork floats on a pond as ripples pass it. Another cork floats down a river on the current. Which one shows a wave carrying energy, and why is the other not a wave? [3]

steps.working: Pond: each ripple lifts the cork and lets it fall as the ripple moves across, and the cork stays where it was.
steps.decision: The water vibrates about a fixed point, across the way the ripple travels; only the disturbance moves on.

steps.working: So the ripple carries energy across the pond without carrying the water with it.
steps.decision: That is what a wave is: energy passed along by vibrations.

steps.working: River: the cork is carried downstream by the water itself.
steps.decision: The near miss: the water flows, so matter travels, and nothing vibrates about a fixed point, so this is not a wave.

prompt: In a transverse wave the particles vibrate at ______ angles to the direction the wave travels.
explain: The cork in the See it bobs up and down while the ripple moves across the pond: the vibration runs across the direction of travel. Across means at right angles, so the word is right; perpendicular or 90° say the same.

twin.prompt: A wave carries ______ from one place to another, but not the material it passes through. (one word)
twin.explain: In the See it the ripple moves energy across the pond while the cork stays put: a wave transfers energy, not matter.

md: Push and pull a slinky along its own length and the vibration runs **along** the direction the wave travels: a **longitudinal** wave. The coils bunch into **compressions** and spread into **rarefactions**, and those regions travel along while each coil shuffles back and forth about the same place. **Sound** and **ultrasound** are the specification's longitudinal examples; ultrasound is sound above 20 000 Hz, too high to hear.

stem: Ultrasound and ultraviolet are both used in hospitals. Sort each into transverse or longitudinal, and describe how the particles move in the longitudinal one. [3]

steps.working: Ultrasound is sound too high to hear, so it is longitudinal.
steps.decision: A sound stays a sound at any frequency: its family is set by how it vibrates, not by its pitch.

steps.working: Ultraviolet is an electromagnetic wave, so it is transverse.
steps.decision: The near miss: the names start alike, but ultraviolet sits beside visible light in the electromagnetic spectrum.

steps.working: In the ultrasound the particles vibrate backwards and forwards along the direction the wave travels.
steps.decision: They bunch up and spread out as the wave passes, then return to where they started.

title: GCSE Physics Revision "Transverse and Longitudinal Waves"
why: Freesciencelessons on the two families and the measuring words, beside our own steps.

prompt: Which of these is a longitudinal wave?
explain: Step 1 of the See it: anything that is sound, whatever its pitch, vibrates along the direction it travels. Water waves, and radio waves, which are electromagnetic, are transverse. The answer: a sound wave in air.

optionNotes.why: A water wave lifts the surface up and down while it travels across, so it is transverse.
Radio waves are electromagnetic, and every electromagnetic wave is transverse.

twin.prompt: Which of these is a transverse wave?
twin.explain: Light is electromagnetic, so it is transverse. Ultrasound and a drum's sound are both sound, which is longitudinal whatever its pitch, as step 1 of the See it says.

optionNotes.why: Ultrasound is only sound too high to hear, so it is longitudinal like any other sound.
A drum pushes the air back and forth along the direction the sound travels: longitudinal.

prompt: Which pair of regions belongs to a longitudinal wave?
explain: Step 3 of the See it: in a longitudinal wave the particles bunch up and spread out along the line of travel. The bunched regions are compressions and the spread regions are rarefactions; crests and troughs belong to a transverse wave.

optionNotes.why: Crests and troughs are the high and low points of a transverse wave, where the vibration runs across the direction of travel.
A normal is the line drawn at right angles to a surface in light diagrams; it is no part of a wave.

twin.prompt: Which pair of words belongs to a transverse wave?
twin.explain: A transverse wave moves the material up and down across its direction of travel, making high points, crests, and low points, troughs. Compressions and rarefactions are the bunched and spread regions of a longitudinal wave.

optionNotes.why: Those are the bunched and spread regions of a longitudinal wave, where the vibration runs along the direction of travel.
Normals and rays belong to light diagrams in optics, not to the shape of a wave.

caption: A displacement–distance graph is the whole wave frozen at one instant.

md: **Amplitude** is the greatest displacement of a particle **from its rest position**: the height of a crest above the middle line, not crest to trough. **Wavelength** ($\lambda$, in m) is one complete wave: crest to crest, or compression to compression. On a graph of displacement against **distance** the whole wave is frozen at one instant, so both can be read straight off it.
Amplitude and wavelength are independent: shaking harder makes taller crests, not longer waves. Only a change of frequency, or of the material, changes the wavelength.

stem: The graph shows a rope wave, displacement in centimetres against distance along the rope in metres. Find its amplitude and its wavelength. [2]

steps.working: The crests reach 5 cm above the middle line and the troughs 5 cm below it.
steps.decision: Find the rest position first: the line the rope sits on with no wave.

steps.working: Amplitude $= 5$ cm
steps.decision: From the rest position to a crest; the 10 cm from trough to crest is two amplitudes.

steps.working: One complete wave runs from 0 m to 2.5 m along the distance axis, so the wavelength is 2.5 m.

task: Set the end to no end and the damping to none. Raise the amplitude and watch the distance between crests; then raise the frequency instead and watch it again.

prompt: A rope wave is plotted on a displacement–distance graph. From a crest down to the next trough measures 9 cm. What is the amplitude, in cm?
explain: Step 2 of the See it: the amplitude runs from the rest position to a crest, and crest to trough is two amplitudes. So the amplitude is $9 \div 2 = 4.5$ cm.

twin.prompt: On another rope wave the troughs sit 7 cm below the rest position. What is the amplitude, in cm?
twin.explain: The amplitude is measured from the rest position, up to a crest or down to a trough: 7 cm.

prompt: A wave is sent along a string. Its amplitude is raised and its frequency is left unchanged. What happens to its wavelength?
explain: Amplitude and wavelength are independent, as the simulation shows: a bigger shake makes taller crests, not longer waves. With the frequency unchanged the crests are just as far apart. The answer: it stayed the same.

optionNotes.why: Taller crests can look as if they spread out, but the crest-to-crest distance is set by the frequency, not by how hard you shake.
Only a higher frequency packs the crests closer together; raising the amplitude leaves their spacing alone.

twin.prompt: The paddle in a ripple tank keeps its rate but moves through half the height. What happens to the ripples?
options: the crests stay the same distance apart
twin.answer: the crests stay the same distance apart
twin.explain: A smaller movement makes a smaller amplitude, lower crests, but the paddle's rate sets the frequency and so the spacing: the crests stay the same distance apart.

optionNotes.why: Crests close up only when the frequency rises; the paddle's rate has not changed.
A lower amplitude changes the height of the crests, not their spacing.

caption: A displacement–time graph follows one point; crest to crest along the time axis is one whole wave.

md: **Frequency** ($f$, in Hz) is the number of complete waves passing a point each second. A graph of displacement against **time** follows one particle, so it shows the time for one complete wave, called the **period** ($T$, in s), crest to crest along the time axis. Then $f = 1 \div T$. Counting works too: waves passed ÷ seconds taken.

title: Why two identical-looking graphs mean different things
md: Read the label along the bottom first. Displacement against **distance** is a photograph of the whole wave frozen in place, so it shows the **wavelength**. Displacement against **time** watches one particle, so it gives the **frequency**. Both show the amplitude up the side.

stem: A crest of a sea wave passes a harbour post every 5 s. Calculate the frequency of the wave. [2]

steps.working: Time for one complete wave, $T = 5$ s
steps.decision: Crest to crest is one whole wave, so this is the period.

steps.working: $f = 1 \div T$
steps.decision: Write the equation before any number: frequency is waves per second.
Below 1 Hz, as it must be for a wave that takes longer than a second.

steps.working: Check: in 60 s, $60 \div 5 = 12$ waves pass, and $12 \div 60 = 0.2$ Hz
steps.decision: Counting waves per second gives the same answer, and is the route when a question counts waves per minute.

prompt: One complete wave passes a buoy every 0.8 s. What is the frequency, in Hz?
explain: Step 3 of the See it: frequency is 1 ÷ the time for one wave. $f = 1 \div 0.8 = 1.25$ Hz, more than 1 Hz because each wave takes less than a second.

twin.prompt: 90 waves pass a harbour wall every minute. What is the frequency, in Hz?
twin.explain: Step 4's route: waves per second. $90 \div 60 = 1.5$ Hz.

alt: A source makes 4 waves each second, each 0.5 metres long, so in one second the front of the wave moves 4 times 0.5 metres.
caption: Speed is how far the front moves in a second: so many waves, each so long.

md: In one second a source makes $f$ waves, each $\lambda$ metres long, so the front of the wave moves $f \times \lambda$ metres every second: that is its speed. **$v = f\lambda$**: speed in m/s, frequency in Hz, wavelength in m. P2 prints no equations, so write it from memory, and write it first: the equation line usually carries a mark.

title: Convert before you substitute
md: The equation gives m/s only if $\lambda$ goes in as metres and $f$ in hertz: centimetres ÷ 100, kilohertz × 1000, waves per minute ÷ 60.

stem: A loudspeaker produces a note of frequency 440 Hz. In the air of the room its wavelength is 75 cm. Calculate the speed of sound in the room. [4]

steps.working: $v = f\lambda$
steps.decision: The equation line first; it is normally a mark of its own.

steps.working: $\lambda = 75 \div 100 = 0.75$ m
steps.decision: Metres in, metres per second out.
Substitute in the equation's own order.
The unit on the answer line; sound in air at about 330 m/s is believable.

prompt: A wave has a frequency of 50 Hz and a wavelength of 0.6 m. What is its speed, in m/s?
explain: As in the See it: $v = f\lambda = 50 \times 0.6 = 30$ m/s. The wavelength is already in metres, so no conversion is needed.

twin.prompt: A wave has a frequency of 6 Hz and a wavelength of 150 cm. What is its speed, in m/s?
twin.explain: Convert first, as step 2 of the See it does: 150 cm = 1.5 m. Then $v = 6 \times 1.5 = 9$ m/s.

md: To find a wavelength or a frequency, rearrange first: $\lambda = v \div f$ and $f = v \div \lambda$. Higher papers give frequencies in kilohertz or in standard form, such as $4.0 \times 10^{4}$ Hz: turn kilohertz into hertz, and key a power of ten with the calculator's exponent button rather than typing zeros. Then ask whether the answer is a sensible size for the wave.

stem: A bat's call has a frequency of 40 kHz. Sound travels at 340 m/s in air. Calculate the wavelength of the call. [4]

steps.working: $v = f\lambda$, so $\lambda = v \div f$
steps.decision: Rearrange before any number goes in.
Kilo means a thousand; the equation needs hertz.
Substitute into the rearranged equation.

steps.working: $\lambda = 0.0085$ m
steps.decision: 8.5 mm: a short wave, which is why a bat can pick out an insect.

title: GCSE Physics - Longitudinal & Transverse Waves - Labelling & Calculating Wave Speed
why: Cognito on labelling a wave and using the wave equation, beside our own steps. It is made for another board; the equation and the units are the same on CCEA's paper.

prompt: A sound of frequency 2 kHz travels through water at 1500 m/s. What is its wavelength, in m?
explain: As in the See it: convert 2 kHz to 2000 Hz, then $\lambda = v \div f = 1500 \div 2000 = 0.75$ m.

twin.prompt: A sound of frequency 5 kHz travels through water at 1500 m/s. What is its wavelength, in m?
twin.explain: $\lambda = 1500 \div 5000 = 0.3$ m. Dividing by 5 instead of 5000 gives 300 m, far too long for a sound of that pitch.

md: **Vibrate, not travel.** Describing particle motion, the mark is for vibrate or oscillate; travel or move scores nothing, and the direction must be at right angles to, or along, the way the wave travels (Summer 2023, 2024 and 2025).
**Letters on a wave.** Distances are lettered and you pick the amplitude: rest line to crest, never crest to trough (Summer 2022 and 2024 Higher).
**Units set by the answer line.** Wavelengths in centimetres, frequencies in kilohertz or standard form, a speed asked in cm/s: convert to fit the line (Summer 2019 to 2025).
**Waves per minute.** Sixty waves a minute is 1 Hz: divide the count by 60, and never hand in the time for one wave as the frequency (Summer 2025 Higher).
**Which graph shows what.** A distance graph gives the wavelength and the amplitude; a time graph gives the frequency and the amplitude (Summer 2023 Higher).

stem: On the lettered wave, four distances are marked A to D. Which letter is the amplitude and which the wavelength? [2]

steps.working: B runs from the rest line up to a crest: B is the amplitude.
steps.decision: Amplitude is measured from the rest position.

steps.working: A runs from a crest down to a trough: two amplitudes end to end, so it is not the amplitude.
steps.decision: The commonest slip on these graphs; halve such a distance if it is all you are given.

steps.working: C runs from one crest to the next: C is the wavelength.
steps.decision: One complete wave, crest to crest.

steps.working: D runs along the line from a crest to the next trough: half a wave, not a wavelength.
steps.decision: Half a wave stops at the trough; a wavelength carries on to the next crest.

prompt: On a drawing of a transverse wave, distance P runs from a crest straight down to the next trough. What does P measure?
explain: Step 2 of the See it: from a crest down to a trough is two amplitudes end to end, one above the rest line and one below. The answer: twice the amplitude, so halve P to get the amplitude.

optionNotes.why: The amplitude stops at the rest line; from crest to trough you have gone a whole amplitude further.
A wavelength is measured along the wave, crest to crest; P is measured up and down.

twin.prompt: On the same drawing, distance Q runs along the rest line from a crest to the next trough. What does Q measure?
twin.explain: Along the line, crest to trough is only half of one complete wave; the wavelength runs on to the next crest, as step 4 of the See it shows. The answer: half a wavelength.

optionNotes.why: A whole wavelength runs from a crest to the next crest; Q stops halfway, at a trough.
The amplitude is measured up and down from the rest line, not along it.

md:
Say what a wave transfers, and tell transverse from longitudinal by how the particles vibrate.
Read amplitude and wavelength off a distance graph, and frequency off a time graph.
Use $v = f\lambda$, writing the equation first and converting units before you substitute.
Rearrange for a wavelength or a frequency, with kilohertz and powers of ten.

Waves usually open the paper: sort waves into the two families, describe how the particles move, read a graph, then a calculation worth three or four marks. The first mark is the equation line; the last is the answer with its unit. Stuck? Write $v = f\lambda$ and put in what you have, in metres and hertz.
